beginner: Tomatillos want soil that drains well and has some compost worked in, but they are not fussy and will do fine in poorer, drier ground than tomatoes tolerate. If water pools on your bed after rain or stays soggy, fix the drainage first, because soggy roots rot. Digging in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting is plenty. Avoid piling on rich manure or heavy nitrogen, which pushes big leafy plants with little fruit.
seasoned: Tomatillos perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with moderate organic matter, but they are markedly less demanding than tomatoes and tolerate lean, dry soils that would stress a tomato. Good drainage is the non-negotiable: waterlogged roots invite root rot. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost in before planting is sufficient. Resist heavy nitrogen or rich manure, which drives rank vegetative growth at the expense of fruit set.

beginner: Soil pH is a measure of acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Tomatillos do well across a fairly wide band, from about 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate soils a little outside that. That makes them easier to place than many crops. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah) often run alkaline (above 7); tomatillos handle the upper end better than most vegetables, but a cheap soil test from your extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Tomatillos are adaptable across roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerate the 5.5 to 7.3 margins better than tomato, one reason they succeed in the alkaline soils of the interior West. As with other Solanaceae, the slightly-acidic-to-neutral band keeps phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium available; strongly acidic soil (below 5.5) raises blossom-end-rot risk through impaired calcium uptake. Most eastern and midwestern soils sit naturally in range.

beginner: Tomatillos are light feeders compared with tomatoes. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed at planting, then sprinkle a small dose around each plant about a month and two months after transplanting. Go easy on nitrogen (the first number on the bag): too much makes a giant leafy plant with few fruit. Once the plant is loaded with fruit, you can stop feeding.
seasoned: A modest feeder. Incorporate a balanced fertilizer at planting, then side-dress lightly at about 4 and 8 weeks. Utah State suggests roughly 1 tablespoon of a nitrogen source per plant at those intervals. Excess nitrogen drives rank vegetative growth and delays fruiting, so keep N moderate and lean toward potassium once flowering begins.

beginner: Time to feed your tomatillos a light dose of balanced fertilizer to keep them productive.
seasoned: Time to side-dress tomatillos lightly; keep nitrogen moderate to favor fruit over foliage.

beginner: Look for the three numbers on the bag (the NPK ratio). A balanced or slightly-higher-potassium blend such as 10-10-10 or 5-10-10 is ideal. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-style fertilizers, which give you leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: balanced to high-K, e.g. 10-10-10 or 5-10-10; avoid high-N

beginner: A small handful, about 1 to 2 tablespoons of balanced fertilizer scratched into the soil 6 inches out from each plant, at about 4 weeks and again at 8 weeks. Water it in and keep it off the leaves and stem. Less is more with tomatillos.
seasoned: About 1 tablespoon of a nitrogen source per plant side-dressed at 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting, per Utah State University Extension, or roughly 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet at the same intervals. Keep granules 6 inches off the stem and water in. Tomatillos need less feed than tomatoes; over-fertilizing with nitrogen is the classic all-leaves-no-fruit mistake.

beginner: Tomatillos get along with the same companions as tomatoes. Basil, marigolds, and nasturtiums are popular neighbors and may help with pests. The most important 'companion' is simply a second tomatillo plant, since they need each other to set fruit. Keep them away from other nightshades (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes), which share their diseases.
seasoned: Tomatillo companion guidance is largely inherited from tomato tradition with little crop-specific extension testing. The marigold/nematode and basil/aromatic-deterrent pairings are the usual suggestions, honestly labeled here as traditional or mechanistic rather than proven for this crop. The one evidence-backed rule is rotational: keep tomatillos away from other Solanaceae to avoid shared disease. And remember the obligate need for a second plant for pollination.

beginner: A traditional good neighbor. Basil's strong scent may keep some pests away, and it grows happily alongside tomatillos.
seasoned: Classic Solanaceae companion; aromatic basil may deter some pests. Traditional, low-risk, not extension-documented for tomatillo specifically.

beginner: Marigolds are a favorite companion. French marigolds can help with soil pests called nematodes, and they brighten the bed and draw in helpful insects.
seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes when grown as a dense planting; the best-documented companion claim in the tomato family, applied here by analogy.

beginner: Fennel releases substances that hold back the growth of many plants around it, so keep it away from tomatillos.
seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and a poor neighbor for most vegetables; the tomatillo interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known habit.

beginner: A slender yellow beetle with three black stripes down its back, often found on tomatillos in particular. The adults and their humpbacked larvae chew ragged holes in the leaves; the larvae carry their own dark excrement on their backs as camouflage.
seasoned: Adults (yellow with three black stripes) and humpbacked larvae skeletonize and hole foliage; larvae mask themselves with frass. Tomatillo is a preferred host.

beginner: Handpick adults and larvae into soapy water, the most effective control in a home garden. Knock egg clusters off leaf undersides. Neem oil helps with heavy larval pressure.
seasoned: Handpick adults, larvae, and orange egg clusters into soapy water. Neem or spinosad for heavy larval populations. Row cover until bloom (then remove for pollinators).

beginner: Check plants early and often, especially leaf undersides, and remove the first beetles before they build up. Clearing nightshade weeds nearby removes alternate hosts.
seasoned: Scout early, destroy first arrivals and egg masses, and eliminate volunteer nightshade hosts. Rotation reduces overwintering carryover.

beginner: A striped leaf beetle that favors tomatillo and other husk-tomatoes more than it bothers tomato.
seasoned: Lema daturaphila (three-lined potato beetle), a chrysomelid leaf beetle specializing on Solanaceae, notably the husk-tomatoes.

beginner: Large green caterpillars, up to 4 inches, with a horn on the rear. They strip leaves fast and leave dark pellets of frass below; you often spot the damage before the well-camouflaged caterpillar.
seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata/sexta larvae defoliate rapidly; large green larvae with a caudal horn, frass below feeding sites.

beginner: Handpick (a UV flashlight at night makes them glow). Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is effective on younger larvae. Leave any hornworm covered in white cocoons, those are parasitic wasps doing your work.
seasoned: Handpick; Bt (B. thuringiensis kurstaki) on early instars; spare wasp-parasitized larvae as a biocontrol reservoir.

beginner: Till in fall to disrupt overwintering pupae. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering insectary plants. Scout for frass.
seasoned: Fall tillage destroys soil pupae; insectary plantings support Cotesia parasitoids; routine frass scouting.

beginner: The larva of a large sphinx moth; a few can defoliate a plant quickly.
seasoned: Hornworm sphinx-moth larvae, shared across Solanaceae.

beginner: Tiny black beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and pepper the leaves with small round shot-holes. Worst on young transplants; established tomatillos shrug off the damage.
seasoned: Numerous tiny shot-holes from Epitrix/Phyllotreta adults; thresholds matter mainly at the seedling stage.

beginner: Floating row cover over young plants, kaolin clay, or spinosad if pressure is heavy. Most established plants outgrow the damage and need no treatment.
seasoned: Row cover until established, kaolin clay film, spinosad under heavy pressure.

beginner: Protect transplants with row cover early. Keep plants vigorous; clean up nightshade weeds and debris where adults overwinter.
seasoned: Early row cover, weed sanitation, and plant vigor; tomatillos tolerate moderate feeding damage.

beginner: Several small Solanaceae-feeding beetles; cosmetic on a vigorous plant but stressful to seedlings.
seasoned: Solanaceous flea beetles overwintering in debris and field margins.

beginner: Fat gray-brown caterpillars that hide in the soil by day and chew through the stems of fresh transplants at the soil line overnight, toppling them.
seasoned: Noctuid larvae (Agrotis spp.) sever transplants at the soil line during the establishment window.

beginner: Push a cardboard or foil collar an inch into the soil around each transplant. Handpick at night. Bt or diatomaceous earth around stems helps.
seasoned: Stem collars, evening handpicking, Bt, diatomaceous-earth barriers.

beginner: Clear weeds and crop debris before planting; collars on every transplant; cultivate the bed ahead of setting plants to expose larvae.
seasoned: Pre-plant weed/residue removal and shallow cultivation; collar each transplant.

beginner: Night-feeding moth larvae that sever young stems at ground level.
seasoned: Cutworm moth larvae in soil and residue.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on growing tips and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky honeydew and ants. Rarely a serious problem on tomatillos.
seasoned: Colonies on new growth and leaf undersides; honeydew and sooty mold possible. Generally minor on this crop.

beginner: Blast off with a water jet; insecticidal soap or neem for stubborn colonies. Marigolds and nasturtiums nearby draw aphid-eating beneficials.
seasoned: Water jet, insecticidal soap or neem on colonies, release or conserve beneficials.

beginner: Avoid excess nitrogen, which makes the soft growth aphids prefer. Encourage ladybugs and lacewings.
seasoned: Limit nitrogen, interplant insectary flowers, support natural enemies.

beginner: Small soft-bodied insects whose numbers can build in warm weather but seldom overwhelm a healthy tomatillo.
seasoned: Multiple aphid species; populations flush in warm weather.

beginner: A white, powdery dusting on the leaves, usually late in the season and in crowded, shaded plantings. It rarely does much harm to a vigorous tomatillo.
seasoned: White powdery colonies on leaf surfaces, favored by warm days and poor air movement; generally low-impact on this crop.

beginner: Improve airflow by spacing and staking; remove the worst leaves. Potassium-bicarbonate or sulfur sprays help if it spreads.
seasoned: Improve canopy airflow, prune affected leaves, apply potassium bicarbonate or sulfur.

beginner: Give plants full sun and wide spacing, and avoid crowding. Good air movement is the main prevention.
seasoned: Full sun, wide spacing, and staking; avoid dense, shaded plantings.

beginner: A fungus that coats leaf surfaces with white powder in warm, dry conditions with poor airflow.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi (e.g. Leveillula/Oidium); UC notes warm sunny exposure suppresses it.

beginner: Dark brown spots with faint target-like rings on the lower, older leaves, which then yellow and drop. Less common and less damaging on tomatillos than on tomatoes.
seasoned: Concentric-ringed Alternaria lesions on older foliage first, advancing upward; lower incidence than on tomato.

beginner: Remove and discard (do not compost) affected leaves. Mulch to stop soil splash. Copper sprays preventively if pressure is high.
seasoned: Sanitation of infected leaves, mulch against splash, preventive copper under pressure.

beginner: Rotate away from nightshades for 3 years, water at the base, and stake to keep foliage off the ground.
seasoned: 3-year Solanaceae rotation, base watering, staking, airflow.

beginner: A soilborne fungus splashed up onto lower leaves in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Alternaria solani, favored by warm wet conditions and overhead moisture.

beginner: Mottled light-and-dark green or yellow patches on leaves, sometimes with puckering or stunting. Spread by aphids and by handling.
seasoned: Mosaic mottling, leaf distortion, and stunting from mosaic and related viruses; roguing is the only response.

beginner: There is no cure: pull and discard infected plants so they do not infect others. Control aphids and wash hands and tools.
seasoned: Rogue and destroy symptomatic plants; manage aphid vectors; sanitize hands and tools.

beginner: Buy healthy plants, manage aphids, avoid handling plants when wet, and do not use tobacco products near the plants.
seasoned: Healthy transplants, vector control, tool/hand hygiene, no tobacco contact.

beginner: Plant viruses (including tobacco/tomato mosaic) carried by insects or on hands and tools.
seasoned: Aphid- and contact-transmitted viruses (TMV/ToMV and others).

beginner: Wilting, blackened lower stems, or sudden collapse, usually where soil stays wet. The most avoidable tomatillo disease, since it comes from soggy ground.
seasoned: Damping-off, crown/root rot, and wilt from Pythium/Phytophthora/Rhizoctonia in saturated soils.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant collapses; remove it. The fix is drainage: never let tomatillos sit in soggy soil.
seasoned: Rogue collapsed plants; correct drainage; avoid overwatering this drought-adapted crop.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds, avoid overwatering, and rotate. Tomatillos prefer it on the drier side.
seasoned: Well-drained or raised beds, moderate irrigation, rotation away from Solanaceae.

beginner: Soilborne fungi that attack roots and stems in waterlogged, poorly drained soil.
seasoned: Soilborne oomycetes and fungi favored by waterlogging and poor drainage.

beginner: Water deeply about once a week once the plants are established, and more often in a heat wave or if they are in pots. Tomatillos handle dry spells better than tomatoes, so you do not need to fuss. Let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and water a bit less once the plant is covered in fruit.
seasoned: About once a week of deep watering once established, more in extreme heat or in containers. Tomatillos develop strong, deep root systems and tolerate short dry spells better than tomatoes, so steady-but-moderate moisture beats frequent shallow watering. Ease off irrigation once fruit has set to concentrate flavor.

beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply so it soaks down 8 to 12 inches rather than just wetting the surface. Deep watering makes the plant tougher in dry weather.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week from rain plus irrigation, wetting the soil 8 to 12 inches deep to reach the main root mass. Deep, less-frequent watering trains roots downward and builds the drought tolerance tomatillos are known for; light surface watering keeps roots shallow and heat-sensitive.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves. A soaker hose or just holding the hose at the base works well. Dry leaves stay healthier. If you have to use a sprinkler, do it in the morning.
seasoned: Water at soil level with a soaker hose, drip line, or hose at the base. Keeping foliage dry limits the foliar diseases tomatillos can get, though they are far less disease-prone than tomatoes. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening.

beginner: Yellow lower leaves and a soggy, never-drying bed are the signs of too much water. Tomatillos like it on the drier side, so soggy roots stress them faster than letting the soil dry a bit between waterings.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and persistently saturated soil indicate roots in oxygen-depleted conditions. Because tomatillos are drought-adapted, overwatering stresses them sooner than underwatering; err toward letting the soil dry between deep waterings.

beginner: Wilting in the afternoon that recovers overnight means the plant is thirsty, though tomatillos wilt less readily than tomatoes. If flowers drop and fruit fails to set during a heat wave, that is usually heat, not thirst, so do not overcorrect with water.
seasoned: Afternoon wilting that recovers overnight signals water stress, though tomatillos resist it well. Distinguish from heat-driven blossom drop (above ~90°F day / below ~55°F night), which water cannot fix and which corrects itself as temperatures moderate.

beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm until the seeds come up. Tomatillos are started indoors, so do not let the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; tomatillo is transplant-started, so do not let the tray surface dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top begin to dry before watering again.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, letting the surface approach dryness between waterings.

beginner: Water deeply at the base, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week soaked well down. Deep watering makes the plant tougher in dry weather. Mulch helps keep the moisture even.
seasoned: After transplant, water deeply at the base, 1 to 1.5 inches a week soaking 8 to 12 inches down; deep, less-frequent watering trains roots downward and builds the drought tolerance tomatillos are known for. Mulch to buffer moisture and suppress weeds.

beginner: Keep the water even from transplant through flowering and the first fruit. Tomatillos handle dry spells better than tomatoes, so err toward letting the soil dry a bit rather than keeping it soggy.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most from transplant through flowering and early fruit set. Keep it even now, though tomatillos resist water stress better than tomatoes and, being drought-adapted, are stressed sooner by overwatering than by a short dry spell.

beginner: Once the plant is covered in fruit, water a little less. Easing off concentrates the flavor; too much water now grows soft, bland tomatillos, so let the top inch dry between deep waterings.
seasoned: The move peculiar to tomatillo: once fruit has set and is sizing, ease off to moderate watering to concentrate the flavor. Tomatillos given too much late water grow soft, bland fruit, so let the top inch dry between deep waterings through the picking run.

beginner: As the weather cools and the plant slows, ease off the water while the last fruit finish.
seasoned: As cool nights slow the plant, water demand drops; taper off as the last fruit finish. Heat-driven blossom drop earlier in the season is a temperature problem, not a watering one, and corrects itself as temperatures moderate.

beginner: A layer of mulch keeps moisture even and weeds down. Once the plant is full of fruit, water a little less for better flavor.
seasoned: Mulch to buffer soil moisture and suppress weeds. Reduce irrigation after fruit set to sharpen flavor; tomatillos given too much late water grow soft, bland fruit.

beginner: The key time for even watering is from transplant through the first flowers and fruit. After that, easing back a little improves flavor.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most from transplant through flowering and early fruit set. Once fruit is sizing, moderate water concentrates flavor.

beginner: These seedlings were raised indoors and have never felt wind or direct sun. Harden them off over 7 to 10 days: start with a couple of hours outside in a sheltered spot, then add time and sun each day. Skip this and the leaves can scorch or the plants sulk for weeks. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F before transplanting, tomatillos are frost-tender.

Start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before your last frost, roughly a week or two after you would start tomatoes. They germinate fast in warm soil (75 to 85°F). When you transplant, you can bury the stem a little deeper than it sat in the pot to encourage extra roots. Remember to start at least two plants so they can pollinate each other.
seasoned: Start indoors 4 to 5 weeks before last frost (about 1 to 2 weeks after tomato). Germinate at 75 to 85°F. Harden off 7 to 10 days; transplant after frost once nights hold above 55°F. Plant slightly deep to encourage adventitious roots. Always set out two or more plants for cross-pollination.

beginner: Use a big pot, at least 5 to 10 gallons, because tomatillos get large. And since you need two plants for fruit, plan on two pots placed near each other.
seasoned: A large, deep container, 5 to 10 gallons minimum per plant; tomatillos are big, sprawling plants. Remember you need at least two plants, so plan two pots set close together.

beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Empty it after watering so the roots are not waterlogged.
seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in pooled water; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

beginner: Use a bagged potting mix made for containers, not garden soil, which packs down in a pot.
seasoned: container_potting_mix

beginner: If the mix feels heavy, stir in about 20% perlite. Add a little slow-release fertilizer at planting.
seasoned: Incorporate 20-25% perlite if dense; modest slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting (tomatillos are light feeders).

beginner: Pots dry out faster than beds, so check daily in summer heat, but tomatillos tolerate drying out a bit between waterings better than tomatoes do.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds; check daily in heat. Tomatillos forgive moderate drought, so err drier rather than waterlogged.

beginner: Container plants need a little regular feeding, but go light on tomatillos: a half-strength balanced liquid feed every few weeks once flowering is plenty.
seasoned: Supplement lightly; a dilute balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks after flowering suffices. Over-feeding nitrogen in a pot gives foliage, not fruit.

beginner: Tomatillos can grow in large containers, but they get big and sprawling, so use a 10-gallon pot with a sturdy cage. The catch: you need at least two plants for them to set fruit, so you will need two pots placed close together. In hot weather container plants dry out fast.
seasoned: Workable in 10-gallon-plus containers with a robust cage, but the obligate cross-pollination requirement means a single pot will not fruit, run two pots side by side. Large plant size makes containers more demanding than for compact crops.

beginner: A self-watering pot is fine, but do not keep it sopping wet; tomatillos like to dry out a little. Water from the top now and then to rinse out built-up minerals.
seasoned: A self-watering container works, but keep the reservoir moderate; tomatillos resent constantly saturated media and prefer a drying cycle. Top-water occasionally to flush salts.

beginner: Most tomatillos you will see are green types like Toma Verde, which are tart and perfect for salsa verde. Purple kinds (Purple De Milpa) are a bit smaller and tangier and turn purple in the husk. Whatever you pick, remember to grow at least two plants, and growing two different varieties together actually improves how much fruit you get.
seasoned: Green market types (Toma Verde, Verde Puebla) are the salsa-verde standard. Purple De Milpa is smaller, tangier, and an aggressive self-seeder. Because tomatillos are self-incompatible, interplanting two different varieties improves cross-pollination and yield. Note that 'pineapple ground cherry' (Physalis pruinosa/peruviana) is a sweeter, smaller relative grown the same way but is botanically distinct from the tart tomatillo.

beginner: Do not plant tomatillos where you grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, or other tomatillos last year. They are all in the nightshade family and share the same soil diseases, which build up if you plant them in the same spot year after year.
seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, other tomatillos, all share Solanaceae soilborne diseases

beginner: Keep a 3-year gap before planting any nightshade in the same spot. One quirk: tomatillos drop fruit that sprouts on its own next spring, so you may get surprise seedlings in last year's bed. Pull them if you are trying to rotate.
seasoned: Rotate on a 3-year cycle away from all Solanaceae. Note that tomatillos self-seed freely from dropped fruit, so last year's bed often sprouts volunteers, pull them if they violate your rotation.

beginner: Tomatillos keep for a week or two on the counter if you leave the papery husks on, which protect the fruit. Keep them in a single layer out of the sun, and do not peel or wash them until you are about to cook.
seasoned: Up to a week or two at cool room temperature with the husks left on. The husk is a natural wrapper that slows moisture loss. Keep them in a single layer out of direct sun. Do not husk or wash until you are ready to use them.

beginner: Pop them in a paper bag (husks on) in the fridge and they will keep 2 to 3 weeks, sometimes longer. Tomatillos, unlike tomatoes, are fine in the fridge. A cool pantry around 50 to 60°F keeps them even longer.
seasoned: Refrigerate husk-on in a paper bag for 2 to 3 weeks; some hold a month or more. Unlike tomatoes, tomatillos are not harmed by refrigeration. For long keeping, store at 50 to 60°F with about 60% humidity, where they last for months.

beginner: To keep them for months, peel off the husks, wash, and freeze the whole fruit in sealed bags. Frozen tomatillos are perfect for salsa verde and cooked sauces later, good for 8 to 12 months.
seasoned: Freeze for months: husk, wash, and freeze whole or sliced in sealed bags. They freeze well for cooked uses like salsa verde and sauces, holding 8 to 12 months.

beginner: Always store them with the husks on; the husk is what keeps them fresh. Peel and rinse off the sticky coating only when you are ready to cook.
seasoned: Store husk-on; the calyx is the fruit's natural protective wrapper. Husk and wash off the sticky resin only at use. A sticky surface under the husk is normal, not spoilage.

beginner: Indeterminate (as explained earlier in this guide) means the plant keeps growing and producing fruit all season long, rather than ripening everything at once and stopping. Almost all cherry tomato varieties work this way, which is part of why they're productive over such a long window. Because they keep growing, they need a sturdy cage or stake to stay upright. A few compact varieties like Tumbling Tom are determinate (they set fruit and stop), which makes them better choices for small containers or hanging baskets.
seasoned: Cherry tomatoes are almost always indeterminate: they grow, flower, and fruit all season until frost kills them. No stopping needed, but they need strong staking or caging. Some compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Patio Choice) are technically determinate.

beginner: Tomatillo seeds sprout fast in warm soil, about 75 to 85°F. A seedling heat mat helps. Cover the tray with a clear lid until shoots appear, then remove it. Sow at least two plants, you need them for pollination.
seasoned: Hold soil at 75 to 85°F for fast, even germination; a heat mat helps. Dome until emergence. Always start two or more plants for cross-pollination.

beginner: A tiny white root, then a pale looped shoot pushing up, which straightens as the first two seed-leaves open.
seasoned: Radicle emergence, then hypocotyl arch lifting the cotyledons; rapid in warm media.

beginner: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

beginner: Give seedlings bright light so they do not get leggy. Pot up if they outgrow their cells. Start hardening off before transplanting, and wait until nights stay above 55°F.
seasoned: Strong light to prevent stretch; pot up as needed. Harden off 7 to 10 days. Transplant after frost once nights hold above 55°F.

beginner: True leaves that look different from the first round seed-leaves, and a sturdy little plant.
seasoned: First true leaves expanding; stem caliper thickening; readiness for hardening off.

beginner: How are your seedlings looking?
seasoned: How are your seedlings looking?

beginner: Once planted out and growing, give each plant a cage or stake, they sprawl to 3 to 4 feet. Water deeply about weekly and feed lightly. Keep two plants close so bees can cross-pollinate them.
seasoned: Cage or stake at transplant (plants reach 3 to 4 ft and sprawl). Deep weekly water, light feeding. Ensure two-plus plants are within pollinator range.

beginner: Fast, bushy growth and the plant filling out its cage. Lots of small yellow flowers will follow.
seasoned: Rapid vegetative bulk-up and branching; onset of flowering follows.

beginner: Is your plant filling out and starting to flower?
seasoned: Is your plant filling out and starting to flower?

beginner: Small yellow flowers with dark centers appear. This is when cross-pollination matters: with two plants nearby, bees will set the fruit. Do not spray insecticides during bloom. Husks form first, then the fruit swells inside.
seasoned: Yellow bell flowers open; insect cross-pollination between plants sets fruit. Protect pollinators (no bloom-time sprays). Empty husks form first, then fill, the diagnostic of successful set.

beginner: Yellow flowers, then small papery husks (lanterns) forming. At first the husks are empty; if pollination worked, fruit swells to fill them.
seasoned: Anthesis, then calyx (husk) expansion; fruit fill confirms pollination. Persistent empty husks signal pollination failure (often a lone plant).

beginner: Are the husks starting to fill with fruit?
seasoned: Are the husks starting to fill with fruit?

beginner: Pick when the fruit fills the husk and the husk starts to split and turn tan, while the fruit is still firm and green for tart flavor. Check weekly, and pick up any that drop, the husk keeps them fresh.
seasoned: Harvest at husk-fill/split, firm and green for peak tartness. Weekly picking; gather dropped fruit (husk-protected and still good).

beginner: Husks splitting open and turning tan, with firm fruit filling them. Fruit on the ground inside intact husks is fine to collect.
seasoned: Calyx split and tan, fruit firm and filling the husk; abscised fruit on the soil remains sound within the husk.

beginner: Have you started harvesting?
seasoned: Have you started harvesting?

beginner: The first frost kills tomatillos. Pick everything usable before a freeze, husk-on fruit stores for weeks. Pull the plants and clear debris. Expect surprise volunteer seedlings next spring from any fruit you missed.
seasoned: Frost terminates the crop. Final harvest before freeze (husk-on storage extends use). Remove plants and residue; anticipate volunteers from dropped fruit next season.

beginner: Plants blackened by frost. Lots of husk-on fruit you can still store, and dropped fruit that may sprout next year.
seasoned: Frost kill; salvageable husk-on fruit for storage; self-seeded volunteers likely the following spring.

beginner: Have you cleared the bed for the season?
seasoned: Have you cleared the bed for the season?

seasoned: Time to start your tomatillos indoors

beginner: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the right window to start tomatillo seeds indoors. Sow at least two plants (two varieties is even better), because a single tomatillo cannot pollinate itself. Plant a couple of seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep, keep them warm (75 to 85°F), and cover until they sprout.
seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the window to start tomatillos indoors. Start two or more plants for cross-pollination. Keep soil at 75 to 85°F and cover until emergence.

beginner: Start introducing your tomatillos to the outdoors

beginner: Expect roughly 2 to 3 pounds of fruit per plant, often more in a long warm season. They keep producing right up until frost. Just remember: a single plant yields almost nothing, so the per-plant figure assumes you have at least two.
seasoned: About 2 to 3 pounds of fruit per plant over the season, and a vigorous plant in a long-season climate can exceed that. Production is continuous from first set until frost. Remember the yield is zero without a second plant for cross-pollination.

beginner: At their peak, two tomatillo plants can bury you in fruit, gardeners are famous for having too many. Pick about once a week, and gather the ones that drop, since the husk keeps them good for days.
seasoned: At peak a healthy plant sets fruit faster than you can use it, hence the tomatillo's reputation for overwhelming the gardener. Pick weekly; fallen fruit holds in its husk.

beginner: Your first year, the biggest factor in success is simply planting two or more plants so they pollinate, after that, tomatillos are forgiving. Give them full sun, room to sprawl, and a cage, and you will likely have plenty.
seasoned: First-season yield hinges far more on having multiple plants for cross-pollination than on fine-tuning culture; tomatillos are otherwise low-maintenance and heat-tolerant. Full sun, wide spacing, and support carry the crop.

beginner: Your plant flowered like crazy but set little or no fruit, just lots of empty papery husks. The number-one cause is growing only one plant. Tomatillos cannot pollinate themselves, so you need at least two plants near each other for bees to cross-pollinate them. The other cause is a heat wave: above about 90°F, flowers drop before setting, which corrects itself when it cools. For next time, always plant two or more, and place them within a few feet so pollinators move between them.
seasoned: Heavy bloom with persistent empty husks is the classic tomatillo failure, and it is almost always self-incompatibility: a lone plant cannot self-pollinate, so no fruit fills the calyx. Two or more plants within pollinator range resolve it. The secondary cause is thermal: flower and pollen viability fall above ~90°F day / below ~55°F night, causing transient blossom drop that recovers as temperatures moderate. Bee activity (avoid bloom-time sprays) is the third lever.

beginner: Lots of flowers (or empty husks) but no fruit
seasoned: Poor or no fruit set (empty husks)

beginner: Plant at least two tomatillos, ideally two different varieties, within a few feet of each other, and keep the planting open to bees (no insecticide sprays during bloom). If a heat wave hits, just wait it out, fruit set resumes as temperatures drop.
seasoned: Always interplant two-plus plants (different varieties ideal) within a few feet; protect pollinators. Expect transient heat-driven blossom drop in extreme weather and do not mistake it for a cultural problem.

beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a cold night. Tomatilloes have no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't built up a protective waxy coating yet. It's tempting to think the plant just needs time to recover, but if it was hit by frost, it usually won't come back. For next time: wait until both your nighttime lows and your soil temperature are reliably above 60°F before transplanting.
seasoned: Tomatilloes are warm-season crops with tropical origin and have no cold tolerance mechanism, unlike brassicas or root vegetables, they cannot harden or acclimate to cold. Chilling injury begins below 50°F and cell damage accelerates near freezing; a single frost event at the transplant stage usually kills the plant outright because young transplants have not yet developed the protective waxy cuticle layer that provides some buffer in established plants. Soil temperature is as important as air temperature: roots in cold soil (below 60°F) cannot take up water or nutrients efficiently even when air temperatures are acceptable, which causes transplant shock that looks like cold damage but persists for weeks after the weather improves.

beginner: Frost or cold damage
seasoned: Frost or cold damage

beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting, checking soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June no matter what the calendar says.
seasoned: Wait until both nighttime air temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. Check soil temperature with a probe thermometer 2-3 inches deep in the actual planting bed, as a south-facing raised bed can be 10°F warmer than a shaded in-ground bed on the same day. In zones 3-5, this means waiting until late May or even early June, regardless of calendar date.

beginner: Tomatillo plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomatillo, it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.
seasoned: Two of the most common problems, blight and blossom end rot, are frequently misdiagnosed and mistreated. Blight (early or late) is a fungal or oomycete disease that enters through wet leaf surfaces; spores splash up from soil and spread rapidly in warm, humid conditions, progressing from lower leaves upward. Removing affected leaves immediately slows but does not stop spread once established. Blossom end rot presents as a sunken, dark patch on the blossom end of developing fruit. Despite appearances, it is not a fungal disease and adding calcium to the soil rarely fixes it. The actual mechanism is calcium transport failure: calcium moves into developing fruit through the water stream in the xylem, and when watering is inconsistent, especially dry periods followed by heavy irrigation, the transpiration-driven flow to the blossom end is interrupted, and those cells die. Steady moisture at the root zone is the only reliable fix.

beginner: Pests or disease
seasoned: Pests or disease

beginner: Water at the base of the plant (not from overhead) and stake the plant for good airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain are far harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatillos to a different bed each year; blight spores can persist in the soil and on old plant material. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small, frequent amounts.
seasoned: Water at the base, never overhead, to eliminate the splash route that delivers blight spores to leaves. Stake and prune for airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain or dew are far less vulnerable. Rotate tomatillos to a different bed each year; blight spores persist in soil and on plant debris, and a fresh location breaks the inoculum cycle. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily to buffer moisture swings, and water deeply and consistently rather than shallowly and frequently.

beginner: Yellow lower leaves and wilting, even when the soil is wet, are the signs you've overwatered. Soggy soil pushes out the air the roots need to breathe; once roots suffocate, the plant can't take up water even though there's plenty of it, which is why it wilts. People often respond by watering more, which makes things worse. Cracked fruit is a related but separate problem: it happens when you water heavily after a dry stretch, the tomatillo swells fast and the skin splits. The fix is consistency: aim for steady moisture rather than long dry spells followed by big waterings.
seasoned: Waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen roots need for cellular respiration, so roots in anaerobic conditions die back, and without functioning roots the plant cannot take up water or nutrients even as the soil stays wet. Yellowing lower leaves are the first visible sign, followed by generalized wilting that paradoxically looks like drought. Fruit cracking is a related but distinct problem: it happens when a sudden surge of water (heavy rain after a dry period, or a large irrigation after letting the plant get too dry) causes rapid fruit cell expansion in a skin that has already stopped stretching. The skin splits at the shoulders or develops concentric cracks. Both problems are rooted in inconsistency rather than sheer total volume, as a plant that receives consistent 1-2 inches per week rarely cracks or shows root oxygen stress.

beginner: Too much water
seasoned: Too much water

beginner: Water deeply and less often rather than a little every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down where the soil stays more stable; roots near the surface are the first to suffocate or dry out. A 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings.
seasoned: Water deeply and less frequently rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering (wetting the soil to 8-10 inches) encourages roots to grow down where soil moisture is more stable; shallow watering concentrates roots at the surface where they are most vulnerable to both drought and saturation. Mulching 2-3 inches around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings, which is the single most effective intervention against both fruit cracking and blossom end rot.

beginner: Flowers dropping before they form fruit and dark sunken patches on the bottom of tomatillos are the two big signs of insufficient or uneven watering. When water gets cut off during flowering, the plant sheds its flowers to conserve resources, physically cutting them loose at the stem. The dark patch on the fruit's base is called blossom end rot; it looks like a nutrient problem but it's almost always caused by uneven soil moisture, not a lack of calcium in your soil. People often add calcium supplements, but that won't fix it; steady, consistent watering will. Note that heat above 90°F causes the same flower-drop, so both can happen at the same time.
seasoned: Water stress during flowering triggers an abscission response: the plant activates an enzyme-driven separation layer at the base of each flower stem, dropping the flower before fruit can form. The same response is triggered by extreme heat (above 90°F daytime, below 55°F nighttime), which means during a heat wave, blossom drop can occur even if the soil seems adequately moist. During fruit development, inconsistent soil moisture is the primary cause of blossom end rot: calcium is transported to developing fruit through the transpiration stream, and interrupted water flow to the blossom end kills those cells. The external result is a sunken, darkened patch on the fruit's base.

beginner: Not enough water
seasoned: Too little water

beginner: Aim for 1 to 2 inches of water per week, delivered consistently. Mulch around the base with straw or shredded leaves to slow the soil from drying out. In hot climates (Zones 8 to 11), a drip line on a timer is the most reliable way to keep moisture steady without thinking about it every day.
seasoned: Aim for 1-2 inches of water per week delivered consistently. Mulch heavily around the base to buffer the soil against rapid drying, as a 2-3 inch layer of straw or shredded leaves can halve moisture loss on a hot day. In zones 8-11, where summer heat makes consistent moisture especially difficult, a drip system on a timer is the most reliable tool. Water at the base of the plant, never the leaves.

beginner: If your plant grows tall and leafy but produces very little fruit, or pale, flavorless tomatillos, sun is probably the problem. Tomatilloes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day; below that, the plant puts its energy into growing stems and leaves instead of fruit. What fruit does form tends to be bland because sugar development depends on sunlight. A secondary sign: shaded plants tend to stay wet longer and get more disease, because leaves don't dry out well in low light. If your spot gets 4-5 hours, you'll get some fruit, but manage expectations: fewer tomatillos, smaller, and less sweet than a full-sun plant.
seasoned: Tomatilloes are among the most light-demanding vegetables: photosynthesis is the energy source for both vegetative growth and fruit sugar development, and fruit quality is directly proportional to the plant's photosynthetic output. Below 6 hours of direct sun, the plant redirects what energy it has toward survival, stem elongation and leaf area, rather than reproduction. Fruit set drops sharply, and what fruit does form is typically thin-skinned, pale, and bland. A secondary effect is increased disease: shaded plants stay wetter longer after rain or irrigation, and poor airflow through dense, etiolated growth creates the humid microclimate that blight and leaf mold need to establish.

beginner: Not enough sun
seasoned: Not enough sun

beginner: Tomatilloes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day, and this is not negotiable. If your current spot is borderline, walk your garden at different times of day and look for a spot a few feet over that gets more morning sun before something shades it. Compact cherry tomatillo varieties like dwarf or patio types tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.
seasoned: Tomatilloes are not negotiable on sun requirements. Below 6 hours of direct sun, expect significantly reduced yields and higher disease pressure regardless of everything else done correctly. If the current spot is marginal (6-7 hours), it is worth mapping sun across the garden before committing the bed again, as a spot that gets shade from a fence or tree in the afternoon may have 2-3 more hours of morning sun available just a few feet away. Dwarf or patio-type cherry tomatillos tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.

beginner: Tomatillos are the tart little green fruits in a papery husk that make salsa verde. You grow them almost exactly like tomatoes: start seeds indoors, then plant them out after the last frost. Three things make them different. You must grow at least two plants, because a single tomatillo cannot pollinate itself and will give you empty husks. The plants get big and sprawling, 3 to 4 feet across, so give them room and a cage or stake to lean on. And they shrug off summer heat and dry spells better than tomatoes, with fewer disease problems. Pick the fruit when it fills out its husk and the husk starts to split. They are very productive, and any fruit that drops will often sprout on its own next spring.
seasoned: The tomatillo (Physalis philadelphica) is a warm-season Solanaceae grown for its tart, husk-covered fruit, the green base of salsa verde. Culture mirrors tomato, started indoors and transplanted after frost, with three differences worth knowing. First, it is self-incompatible: a single plant sets almost no fruit, so grow at least two for cross-pollination. Second, the plant is large, sprawling, and vigorous, reaching 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, so it needs a sturdy cage or stake and wide spacing. Third, it tolerates summer heat and drought better than tomato and is notably less disease-prone, which makes it forgiving across hot regions. Fruit is ready when it swells to fill, and often split, its papery husk. Plants are heavy bearers and self-seed readily from dropped fruit, so expect volunteers the following spring.

beginner: One planting produces tomatillos all season until frost, no need to replant. In hot regions (the low desert, South Florida) growers run a separate spring crop and fall crop around the worst summer heat, but in most gardens it is one long crop.
seasoned: Not a succession crop: one indeterminate planting bears continuously until frost. Desert and tropical regions split into spring and fall crops around a summer heat pause.

beginner: Watch the husk. A tomatillo is ready when the fruit grows big enough to fill the papery husk and the husk starts to split open and turn tan. For the tart green flavor you want in salsa, pick while the fruit is still firm and green; if you wait too long it turns yellow and goes soft and mild. Ripe fruit comes off easily, and a lot of it simply falls to the ground, where the husk keeps it fresh for a few days. Check your plants about once a week and pick as the fruit fills out.
seasoned: Pick when the fruit swells to fill its papery husk and the husk begins to split, turning from green toward tan. For bright, tart fruit (the classic salsa-verde flavor) harvest while the fruit is still firm and green; left longer it turns yellow, soft, and blandly sweet. Ripe fruit detaches easily and often drops to the ground on its own, where it keeps for days inside the protective husk. Harvest over the whole season as fruit fills out, roughly weekly at peak.

beginner: In cold areas, tomatillos are a summer crop. Start seeds indoors, plant out after your last frost, and pick from midsummer until frost. They love the heat of summer and need no break. Grow at least two plants so they pollinate each other.
seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 to 7) grows tomatillo as a single frost-bracketed summer crop. Start indoors, transplant after the last frost once nights hold above 55°F, and harvest from midsummer until the first fall frost ends the season. The heat-tolerant tomatillo runs straight through summer with no pause. Plant two or more for pollination.

beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, tomatillo is a two-season crop. Plant Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest weeks of summer: the plant just does not perform well in the worst of the heat, so most Valley gardeners skip it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
seasoned: Tomatillo in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Feb 14 - Mar 20 for a spring harvest running Apr 20 - Jun 18, then set out again Sep 15 - Oct 15 for a fall harvest running Nov 19 - Dec 15. TAMU AgriLife's Valley planting guidance simply leaves that stretch off the calendar for this crop, rather than asserting a specific heat-failure mechanism. beginner: Tomatillo is a better bet than its nightshade cousins here: it still wants a warm-season start, but it is a bit more forgiving of our cool summer. Start seeds indoors in spring and set transplants out once the soil has warmed, May in the valley and May into June on the milder but cooler-summered coast. Plant at least two so they cross-pollinate, and pick husks from midsummer into fall.
seasoned: Tomatillo is not in OSU's Oregon planting table by name, but WSU's Washington vegetable guide (EM057E) gives it the same transplant profile as tomato, just a shorter 5-to-6-week indoor lead and a somewhat faster 55-to-90-day maturity. This cell models its set-out window on OSU's own tomato entry: a single May window in the Willamette Valley, widening to a later May-into-June window on the coast, the same shape OSU gives tomato itself. Tomatillo tolerates the region's cool nights better than eggplant and keeps setting fruit through summer with no pause; close the harvest display about three weeks ahead of the average first frost, since the season's cooling, wetter fall slows ripening well before an actual freeze. Plant at least two for cross-pollination.

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley you grow tomatillo as a single spring crop only, not the two-crop spring-and-fall pattern used in the Arizona low desert. Start seed indoors in early February, set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past, and pick the papery-husked fruit from mid-June through the end of the month. Once daytime highs pass 90°F in summer the plants stop growing well, so there is a long summer break, and unlike Phoenix a second planting is not set here because frost returns by late November. Tomatillo needs a second plant nearby for pollination either way, so plan for at least two.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) runs tomatillo on one spring cycle, following the UNLV Master Gardener chart's Tomato* row, which covers tomatillo alongside tomato. Seed goes in indoors in early February, about five weeks before the mid-March set-out; transplants set out in mid-March, after the valley's practical last frost (UNR Extension SP-99-11 gives March 15, later at the cooler zone 8 edge, earlier at Laughlin in zone 10). At an 80-day days-to-maturity, fruit ripens from mid-June, then daytime highs past the Fact Sheet FS-02-61 90°F ceiling shut growth down from July into September. This is a delta from the Phoenix low desert, where tomatillo runs a spring-and-fall two-window pattern: Southern Nevada's UNR chart does not carry that second Tomato*-row window, so only the spring cycle is set here. Frost returns around November 25 in zone 9.

seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs tomatillo on one spring cycle, per USU Extension. Seed goes in indoors in late February; transplants set out about April 1, the St. George Group D (Very Tender) date, just after the March 30 average last frost. At an 80-day days-to-maturity, husked fruit fills out from late June, leaving about ten days before daytime highs past the 90°F ceiling shut growth down from July into September. USU does not recommend a fall or second planting for the St. George area; frost returns around November 1. Set out at least two plants since tomatillo is self-incompatible and needs a second plant nearby for pollination.

beginner: Here is the one thing that trips up most first-time tomatillo growers: a single plant will hardly set any fruit, no matter how healthy it looks. Tomatillos cannot pollinate themselves, so you have to grow at least two plants near each other, and two different kinds is even better. Bees carry the pollen from one plant to the other, so plant them within a few feet and let the bees visit. Plant two and you will be giving tomatillos away by late summer.
seasoned: Tomatillo is functionally self-incompatible: a flower will not set fruit with its own pollen, so a lone plant flowers heavily and produces almost nothing, just a few empty husks. Grow at least two plants, ideally two different varieties, close together so insects can move pollen between them. Bees and other pollinators do the work, so keep the planting open to insect traffic and avoid spraying during bloom. This is the single most common reason a tomatillo crop fails. (Utah State University Extension; SDSU Extension; University of Minnesota Extension)

beginner: Good news: tomatillos get sick far less often than tomatoes. They can catch the same things (leaf blights, powdery mildew, viruses, root rot), but usually only mildly. Full sun, well-drained soil, room between plants, and keeping them away from other nightshades head off most trouble, you rarely need to spray.
seasoned: Tomatillo is notably less disease-prone than tomato. It can develop early blight, powdery mildew, mosaic viruses, and root rots, but typically at lower incidence and severity. A sunny, well-drained, well-spaced site plus a 3-year rotation away from Solanaceae prevents most problems; few home growers ever need to spray.
